title: Prediction Machines
subtitle: The Simple Economics of Artificial Intelligence
pitch: Three economists boil AI down to one thing: it makes prediction cheap. Then they show what that does to decisions, jobs and strategy.

chapters.g: When something gets cheaper we use more of it, and its complements rise in value.
Prediction means filling in missing information, which covers far more than forecasting.
Why prediction feels like intelligence to us.
Training, input and feedback data, and when data is worth the cost.
What humans and machines are each good at predicting.
A decision has parts: prediction, judgment, action and outcome.
As prediction gets cheap, deciding what you value becomes more important.
Better prediction lets firms handle more situations instead of simple rules.
Limits of learning from data, such as cause and effect.
When it makes sense to take the human out of the loop.
Breaking jobs into tasks to see where prediction fits.
A canvas for mapping each decision a business makes.
How roles change when parts of them are automated.
AI as a question for strategy, not just IT.
Cases where cheap prediction changes the whole business model.
Bias, quality and security risks for firms using AI.
Wider questions about jobs, inequality and power.

ideas: Cheap prediction raises the value of judgment, data and action.
Decisions can be broken into parts to see where AI fits.
Big wins come when cheap prediction changes the whole strategy.

args.a: Seeing AI as cheap prediction makes it easy to understand and plan for.
args.c: Newer generative and agentic systems act and plan, which this frame may undersell.
If AI also learns judgment from human feedback, that complement may shrink too.

questions: What prediction in your daily life has become cheaper?
Which part of a decision would you never hand to a machine?
Is a language model just a prediction machine?

quiz.q: What does AI make cheap, according to the authors?
What becomes more valuable as prediction gets cheap?
Which is not one of the parts of a decision they describe?
